evidence.claim: Limestone bluffs and river towns link two great river confluences.
evidence.quote: Meeting of the Great Rivers is a breathtaking 33-mile section of the Great River Road, where the great Mississippi, Illinois and Missouri rivers come together.

evidence.claim: Limestone bluffs and river towns
evidence.quote: roadway cradled by the rolling waters of the Mighty Mississippi River and majestic limestone river bluffs.

evidence.claim: two great river confluences.
evidence.quote: The north end of the route is at Pere Marquette State Park, located at the confluence of the Mississippi and Illinois Rivers. The south end of the route is at the Lewis and Clark State Historic Site, located near the confluence of the Mississippi and Missouri Rivers.

evidence.claim: The Meeting of the Great Rivers Scenic Route follows 33 miles of southwestern Illinois river country, with bends along forested bluffs and towns beside the water.
evidence.quote: The 33-mile Meeting of the Great Rivers Byway begins in Hartford at the intersection of Illinois Route 3 and New Poag Road.

evidence.claim: with bends along forested bluffs and towns beside the water.
evidence.quote: Illinois Route 100 leads you through Alton and bends along the forested river bluffs

evidence.claim: Part of the Great River Road, it is also a National Scenic Byway.
evidence.quote: The route has been officially designated as a National Scenic Byway by the Federal Highway Administration. The route coincides with a portion of the Great River Road.

evidence.claim: The Great Rivers & Routes Tourism Bureau emphasizes its scenery, archaeology and history; the Illinois tourism office highlights the roadway between limestone bluffs and the Mississippi.
evidence.quote: The designation of the Meeting of the Great Rivers National Scenic Byway has brought national attention to the spectacular scenery, archeological finds, historic happenings, cultural experiences and memorable recreation.

evidence.claim: the Illinois tourism office highlights the roadway between limestone bluffs and the Mississippi.
evidence.quote: roadway cradled by the rolling waters of the Mighty Mississippi River and majestic limestone river bluffs.

evidence.claim: At Elsah, the opening of the Great River Road in 1964 marked a change for a village that had remained quiet after its shipping trade declined.
evidence.quote: Elsah remained mainly a quiet village until the opening of the Great River Road (Illinois Route 100) in 1964.

evidence.claim: after its shipping trade declined.
evidence.quote: Elsah prospered as the main shipping point for the agricultural goods produced by the farmers of Jersey County. The village's importance diminished with the coming of the railroad

evidence.claim: The scenic route received Illinois designation in 1998.
evidence.quote: The Meeting of the Great Rivers Scenic Route was designated as an Illinois State Scenic Byway on  June 8, 1998.

evidence.claim: National designation followed in 2000, when the corridor was extended from East Alton south to New Poag Road.
evidence.quote: It was later added to the National Scenic Byway program on  June 15, 2000, with an addition that  extended the existing byway from East Alton south to New Poag Road.

evidence.claim: Traveling from the northern end, begin at Pere Marquette State Park and follow the route through Grafton, Elsah and Alton.
evidence.quote: The north end of the route is at Pere Marquette State Park

evidence.claim: follow the route through Grafton, Elsah and Alton.
evidence.quote: The cities and villages of Grafton, Chautauqua, Elsah, Alton, East Alton, Wood River and Hartford are located along the route.

evidence.claim: A parallel bike trail accompanies the road between the park and Alton, with the Confluence Bike Trail continuing toward Hartford.
evidence.quote: The Sam Vadalabene Bike Trail parallels the route between Pere Marquette State Park and Alton. The Confluence Bike Trail parallels the route from Alton south to Hartford.

evidence.claim: At Alton, the corridor includes the Clark Bridge and the National Great Rivers Museum at the Melvin Price Locks and Dam.
evidence.quote: Other major points of interest along the Route include Piasa Park, the Clark Bridge in Alton, and the National Great Rivers Museum  at the Melvin Price Locks and Dam.

evidence.claim: The southern end reaches the Lewis and Clark State Historic Site near the meeting of the Missouri and Mississippi rivers.
evidence.quote: The south end of the route is at the Lewis and Clark State Historic Site, located near the confluence of the Mississippi and Missouri Rivers.

evidence.claim: Pere Marquette’s lodge is a piece of the park’s early history, built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s.
evidence.quote: The park's heart is a Civilian Conservation Corps-built lodge, first built in the 1930s

evidence.claim: The park began in 1931 as Piasa Bluffs State Park and soon took its present name.
evidence.quote: Pere Marquette State Park was founded in 1931 as the Piasa Bluffs State Park, but was soon renamed.

evidence.claim: The lodge was expanded in 1985; a visitor center followed in 1997 with exhibits on local history and ecology.
evidence.quote: later expanded in 1985 to contain 72 rooms. A visitor center, with exhibits on local ecology and history, opened in 1997.

evidence.claim: The Illinois River borders the park on the west and south.
evidence.quote: The Illinois River lies adjacent to the western and southern boundaries of the park.

evidence.claim: In late winter, hundreds of bald eagles congregate in and near the park to catch fish, arriving from wetland nesting areas to the north.
evidence.quote: Hundreds of eagles that nest in the wetland areas to the north congregate in and around the park areas in late winter to catch and eat fish during the cold months.

evidence.claim: Limestone from Grafton’s quarries became part of bridges and public buildings beyond the town’s riverfront.
evidence.quote: The local limestone was used to build the Eads Bridge in St. Louis, government buildings in Rock Island, and the Jersey County Courthouse in Jerseyville.

evidence.claim: Quarries supplied stone for the Eads Bridge in St. Louis and the Jersey County Courthouse, while boatbuilding and commercial fishing supplied other work.
evidence.quote: employment opportunities coming from the local stone quarries, boat building and commercial fishing.

evidence.claim: Quarries supplied stone for the Eads Bridge in St. Louis and the Jersey County Courthouse
evidence.quote: The local limestone was used to build the Eads Bridge in St. Louis, government buildings in Rock Island, and the Jersey County Courthouse in Jerseyville.

evidence.claim: The Old Boatworks south of Main Street included a paint house and machine shop where paddle wheelers and later PT boats were built.
evidence.quote: The Old Boatworks, located south of Main Street, once housed a paint house and a machine shop where paddle wheelers and later PT boats were built.

evidence.claim: The historic district connects Main Street to the river by way of Maple Street and the wharf.
evidence.quote: The district includes two blocks of Main Street (Illinois Route 100) and a section of Maple Street connecting to Grafton's historic wharf on the Mississippi River.

evidence.claim: Built of limestone in 1846, that wharf replaced an earthen landing lost to a flood.
evidence.quote: The limestone wharf was built in 1846 to serve river transport, trade, and entertainment in Grafton; it was the city's second wharf, replacing an earthen wharf that was lost to a flood.

evidence.claim: Elsah’s stone houses began with an offer: James Semple, who founded the village in 1853, gave free lots to people who built with stone from his quarry.
evidence.quote: James Semple, a local lawyer, prominent politician and United States Senator from Illinois, founded Elsah in 1853 and offered free lots to anyone who built houses with stone from his quarry.

evidence.claim: James Semple, who founded the village in 1853,
evidence.quote: founded Elsah in 1853

evidence.claim: The village became a shipping point for Jersey County farm produce, then lost importance as the railroad arrived.
evidence.quote: Elsah prospered as the main shipping point for the agricultural goods produced by the farmers of Jersey County. The village's importance diminished with the coming of the railroad

evidence.claim: Its entire village entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1973.
evidence.quote: In 1973, the entire village was placed on the National Register of Historic Places.

evidence.claim: LaSalle Street’s commercial district extends three blocks inland from the river and consists mainly of stone buildings.
evidence.quote: The historic commercial district on LaSalle Street, which extends three blocks inward from the river, consists mainly of stone buildings

evidence.claim: On Mill Street, residential sections include stone and brick houses and a block of Greek Revival homes.
evidence.quote: The other two districts are both located on Mill Street and are primarily residential; the larger one is three blocks long and has an assortment of stone and brick houses, while the smaller section has a single block of Greek Revival homes.

evidence.claim: LaSalle Street’s historic commercial district is built mainly of stone.
evidence.quote: The historic commercial district on LaSalle Street, which extends three blocks inward from the river, consists mainly of stone buildings

flags: Direction follows the material strip’s increasing miles, from the park through Grafton and Elsah to Hartford. Rosedale and Marshall Landing are context pins, not asserted byway endpoints.

Omitted the current Piasa destruction date: the cache offers dates from 1846–47 through the 1870s and disputes the reliability of later images. Tourism’s traditional-monster account also differs from the detailed Piasa page; no community-authored source is cached.
The park page explicitly credits the CCC for the lodge; Alton calls it WPA-era, which does not establish WPA construction. Retained the specific CCC attribution.
